name: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
title: Board Advisory and Fiduciary Risk
answer: Board advisory and fiduciary risk covers the work of helping directors understand and oversee an organization's use of artificial intelligence. It sits inside corporate governance and regulatory compliance, where fiduciary duties of care and loyalty meet AI-specific risks such as bias, privacy, security, intellectual property, and disclosure. The scope includes advising boards on AI strategy, risk appetite, oversight structures, and the documentation of decisions. The 148 active AI lawsuits tracked on this site, 92 of them intellectual property, show the kinds of disputes that can reach a board's risk register. It also includes the risk that directors themselves face when oversight is alleged to be inadequate.

The scope includes advising boards on AI strategy, risk appetite, oversight structures, and the documentation of decisions. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on board and committee charters, management reporting lines, and a clear allocation of AI oversight among the full board, the audit committee, the risk committee, and any technology or AI committee. It depends on an AI inventory, a compliance program, and a map of legal and regulatory obligations to owners inside the company. The 219 compliance and regulation pages and the 6978 state AI bills tracked here reflect the volume of obligations that a board oversight process may need to monitor. Documentation systems, board portals, and minutes are part of the infrastructure because they create the record of what the board was told and when. Outside counsel, internal audit, and compliance functions often supply the underlying analysis.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through board education, committee briefings, management certifications, and structured risk assessments of AI use cases. Counsel and compliance teams commonly prepare an AI inventory, map each use case to legal and regulatory duties, and present a risk dashboard to the board. Directors ask management for evidence of testing, monitoring, and remediation, and they record their questions and conclusions in minutes. The 29 AI case law precedents tracked here can help frame oversight questions, though the facts of each matter differ. The method is iterative, because AI systems change and the legal landscape shifts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance sit at the center of board advisory work. Shareholders have rights to accurate disclosure and to bring derivative claims, and regulators have enforcement powers over AI-related conduct. The 148 active AI lawsuits tracked here, 92 of them intellectual property, illustrate the litigation exposure that can follow AI deployment. Provenance matters because directors may need to show what they knew about training data, model outputs, and third-party components, and what they did in response. Risk includes reputational harm, regulatory penalties, contractual liability, and personal exposure for directors in oversight cases.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The horizon points toward more board attention, more committee structures, and more documented oversight of AI. The 6978 state AI bills tracked here suggest a continuing patchwork of obligations that boards will need to monitor across jurisdictions. The 29 AI case law precedents will likely grow as courts address oversight, disclosure, and liability questions. Boards may see more requests for AI expertise, more independent directors with technology backgrounds, and more disclosure about AI risks in securities filings. The direction of travel is toward treating AI oversight as a standing fiduciary matter rather than a one-time project.
